extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers interested in writing noir/neo-noir
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating noir (and neo-noir) stories/films, listing the key elements, tropes, stylistic choices, and examples authors can use or subvert when writing in the noir genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: The outsider
rubrics_metrics.description: the noir protagonist is an outcast – perhaps a soldier coming home after the war, a released prisoner or just a stranger in town. Traditionally the lead is male, but a noir such as Mullholland Drive puts women firmly in the centre, so feel free to deviate from the usual. He or she is a dropout, a loser and nobody cares about them and this sense of alienation pervades the whole story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the lead feel alienated and marginalised; their outsider status should pervade the story. You can subvert traditional gender expectations by centering women. Use the protagonist's social disconnection as a driver of mood and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: they may be central to the story, but the noir protagonist is no hero. They are driven by revenge, greed, lust or all of the above and they cross a moral line to get what they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray protagonists as anti-heroes who make morally dubious choices. Maintain reader empathy (give a glimmer of hope) even while letting the character pursue self-destructive aims; the glimmer should be torn away by the end. Avoid conventional heroic arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatalism and Nihilism
rubrics_metrics.description: hope has forsaken the world of noir. This is the American Dream gone wrong... The world-weary noir protagonist is on a fatal path, due to a doom of their own making. Remember, this is not a tragic hero who the fates seem to conspire against, despite their good intentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish an atmosphere of inevitability and moral breakdown. The protagonist’s choices (cheating, stealing, murder, etc.) should set irreversible events in motion. Emphasise the collapse of optimism rather than external fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Femme or Homme Fatale
rubrics_metrics.description: the fatale brings sex and lust into the equation. The attractive stranger appears to be vulnerable or there to help the protagonist, but it turns out he’s just there to seduce and wrong-foot our anti-hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fatale to introduce sexual manipulation and misdirection. Recognise the trope’s familiarity—either play it straight, subvert it (reverse gender roles), or complicate it to avoid cliché. Be mindful of problematic portrayals (see guidance about fetishising dead women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creatures of the Night
rubrics_metrics.description: film noir is associated with the night, when the streetlights reflect on rain-slicked streets and the underworld comes out to play. European directors brought German expressionism to Hollywood—extreme camera angles and high-contrast lighting—which cast angular shadows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use night, lighting, and visual contrast to create atmosphere, especially for visual media. That said, noir can be effective in daylight too (examples: Chinatown, Brick); choose setting/lighting to support mood rather than follow rules slavishly.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person
rubrics_metrics.description: the first-person puts the reader right in the protagonist’s head, which adds to the claustrophobia you need to create for noir. It also allows you to play with the unreliable narrator technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider first-person for immediacy and unreliability, but don’t feel forced—use the POV that best serves the story. If using first-person, exploit the narrator’s potential delusion, confusion, or lies to complicate the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: you don’t need to have a private eye or a world-weary police officer investigating a murder, but these staples still work as an easy way to insert a mystery. Classic noir usually starts with a dead body (usually a woman) or at least a missing person, but neo-noir offers a broader scope (e.g., preventing a murder, an amnesiac piecing together events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mystery elements to drive plot and reveal character. You can broaden the concept beyond traditional murder-investigation plots; the journey and moral consequences are as important as the whodunit.

rubrics_metrics.name: City Streets
rubrics_metrics.description: some may argue that noir has to be in an urban setting, but the author disagrees. While Chandler and Ellroy focus on L.A., neo-noir can use rural, suburban, or international settings (e.g., Scandi-noir) to create similar alienation and desperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t feel limited to urban locales—consider how non-urban settings (rural, suburban, international) can heighten isolation and disquiet. Setting should reinforce theme and tone rather than follow geographic expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken Noses
rubrics_metrics.description: violence is an essential part of the noir tradition. The protagonist will get beaten or roughed up, there are bodies to be buried, and the bad guys will catch up and mete out physical punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include physical danger and consequences to concretise the genre’s darkness. Use violence to signal stakes and the brutal reality of the noir world; avoid gratuitousness unless it serves theme or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: No happy ending
rubrics_metrics.description: noir is the boulevard of broken dreams, so don’t expect to let your protagonist get the guy and skip off into the sunset. Your lead may die, lose everything, or be no further ahead by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with loss, compromise, or moral/psychological defeat rather than tidy resolution. Even if the mystery is solved, ensure the protagonist's situation has not meaningfully improved; avoid conventional redemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pared Back Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: when it comes to noir fiction, keep your prose simple, direct and hard. No florid descriptions. Extended metaphors and overwrought description are discouraged unless doing a period piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt concise, snappy language and pared-down description. Avoid florid, extended metaphors that bog pace; focus on sharp detail and rhythm suited to noir’s tone.
